**On Having a Thousand Words**

A thousand words is a small purse. You can spend it all at once or keep a few coins in your pocket for later. I've been thinking about how people spend words without noticing, how we say "I'm fine" forty times a week and mean maybe three of them. A thousand words, given freely, feels like a kind of luxury, and also a kind of responsibility, because each one has to earn its place.

When I picture someone with exactly this allowance, I picture a kitchen. Morning light, the radiator knocking like it wants to be let in. A woman, my grandmother in some version of my head, though she never had a kitchen like this, is saving the string from a parcel. She winds it around two fingers, then around a cardboard tube, and sets it in a drawer already full of string. Nobody ever needed that much string. But she never threw any of it away, and I've come to think of that drawer as the most honest thing in the house. It was a record of every package that had ever arrived, every small hope that something might be tied up again someday.

Words are a bit like that string. We keep them, we wind them around our fingers, we forget where we put them. Some of the ones I remember best were never important. "Mind the step." "Eat something, you look thin." "We'll see." That last one could mean yes, no, or never, and children learn very quickly to listen for the tone underneath. Language is mostly the tone underneath. The dictionary gives you the coat rack; the voice tells you who's hanging their coat there.

I like the idea of a word budget because it forces a kind of honesty. If you have unlimited space, you pad. You say the thing three times in three slightly different ways, hoping one will land. You wrap the point in tissue paper until nobody can find it. Constraint strips that away. You have to decide what matters. Is this sentence doing work, or is it just keeping me company?

I don't think that's only true of writing. Conversation works the same way. The people I trust most are rarely the most eloquent. They tend to say a little and mean it, and when they're quiet, the quiet has weight. My friend Teodor once spent an entire car ride to the airport saying almost nothing, and when we pulled up to the curb he said, "You're going to be okay," and I believed him more than I'd believed any paragraph of reassurance in my life. Eleven words, maybe. Hard to say; I didn't count.

There's a temptation, when you're given room, to fill it. I notice this in myself. A question arrives and I want to answer it from every side at once, to show that I've considered the objections, the exceptions, the footnotes. Sometimes that's useful. Often it's a way of hiding inside the sentence, of making sure no single claim can be pinned on me. A thousand words forces a stance. You have to stand somewhere and say, this is what I think, roughly, for now.

So here is what I think, roughly, for now. Most of what we say is string. We wind it, we store it, we rarely use it, and we are glad, in the end, that it's there. But the words that matter are the ones we send out on purpose: the apology we finally make, the thank-you we almost forgot, the plain statement of love that feels too simple to say and turns out to be the only thing anyone wanted to hear.

My grandmother, if she were here, would probably tell me to stop being so fancy about it. She would say, "Just say the thing, and then go wash the dishes." And she'd be right. The dishes are waiting, the light is moving across the table, the radiator is knocking again. The budget is nearly spent, and I find I don't mind. A thousand words is enough to say that I was here, that I noticed the string, that small things were kept for reasons we only partly understand.

I'll keep a few coins in my pocket. Some things are better left unspent.
